title: The training principles series: frame & flow
summary: Defines 'frame' (the skeleton: height, clavicle width, waist, hips, joint size, limb length) and 'flow' (how the whole physique ties together aesthetically). Small joints make muscles look bigger; flow hinges mostly on a tight core and balanced limbs. A bodybuilder should assess their frame objectively and pack muscle in the right places to create a finished work of art.

claims.claim: Frame is the skeletal system supporting the muscles and a key genetic factor: the bigger the frame the more muscle it can carry; a 6'6" person has more potential mass than a 5'8" one, though not necessarily a better look.
He has a small frame: very short clavicles, narrow shoulders, and a back and shoulders that lack width.
A short frame has an advantage: muscles stacked on a smaller area pop more, look more 3D and bulkier, but lack width.
Be objective and realistic about your genetics; wide-shouldered people also have potential weak points elsewhere.
Frame also includes waist size, hip width, and the size of wrists, elbows, knees and ankles.

Smaller joints make the surrounding muscle bellies look bigger: a 15-inch forearm looks smaller on a thick wrist; a thick elbow blunts a biceps peak; big knees stop quads from sweeping; thick ankles make calves look worse.
What matters in bodybuilding is the sweep and curvature of the muscle belly relative to the joint.
Bigger structure (wide hips, big joints) gives more strength potential; strongmen usually have wide hips and big legs as a solid platform.
Flow is how the whole frame looks; it is subjective with no objective definition, but aesthetic physiques with a trim waist, wide shoulders and a good V-taper are widely accepted as having flow.
The core (abs, obliques, how the trunk connects to the legs) is what makes or breaks flow, which is why bubble guts and bloated modern bodybuilders drew criticism and the trend is changing.
No one cares if you have massive arms and a gut; a tight core must tie the physique together.
Flow also applies to limbs: massive quads with small calves or big biceps with small forearms kill the flow, so flow partly means balance.
Peripheral areas like neck or calves can lag without hurting flow much, because they don't connect parts of the physique together.
Strive for the best flow possible by objectively assessing your frame and building measurements that make it look as big and great as possible.
His aim in bodybuilding is to pack his skeleton with muscle in the right places to create a finished work of art he can be proud of and others can admire.
Your overall flow matters more than the size of your muscles.
